In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms of the immune response to pathogens and the role of this response in the pathogenesis of infectious and inflammatory diseases.
the study of the mechanisms of the regulation of the immune response in mammals, including humans.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PRRs are a group of receptors that recognize both exogenous and endogenous molecules and trigger immune responses.
PRRs are the main sensors of both pathogen and host danger.
PRR-mediated immune system plays an important role in the defense against pathogens, but is also a key player in the control of cellular homeostasis (1–7).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PRRs are the key players in the innate immune system and are the main sensors of the cellular environment.
we are trying to understand how the immune system detects and responds to pathogens and how it detects and responds to cellular stress.
PRRs can be activated in response to both exogenous (pathogens) and endogenous (DNA lesions) stimuli, and this activation leads to DNA repair.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activation of PRRs is associated with the activation of DNA repair.
PRRs are not only important for the immune system.
the PRR-mediated innate immune response can be also triggered by DNA damage and repair.
